title: 5 Maths Gems #200
author: Jo Morgan
summary: Morgan marks the 200th installment of her long-running 'Maths Gems' series with a curated round-up of new classroom resources, each accompanied by her own evaluative commentary rather than bare links. She walks through MathsPad's self-testing Topic Key Facts Sheets and Grade 9 Club question packs, Andy from m4th5.co.uk's new 'X Why' graphing tool (noting specific features she likes, such as bearings diagrams in non-standard orientations), the NCETM's newly-completed Key Stage 4 geometry professional development materials, a murder-mystery A-level revision task, and two self-marking worksheet sites (esheets.io and Whiteboard Workouts) she had not previously encountered. Beyond the resource round-up, the post includes a substantial reflective 'Milestone' section in which Morgan traces the blog's history from its 2014 launch through the decline of teacher-Twitter as a resource-sharing hub, and an 'Events' section recounting her attendance at the MEI Conference and upcoming plans for the Future of Maths Education event, Mathsconf41, and BCME 10. The piece functions as both a practical resource digest for maths teachers and a first-person account of sustaining a long-running professional blog through the shifting social-media landscape maths teachers rely on for resource-sharing.
points: Each resource entry carries Morgan's own evaluative judgment rather than a bare link -- e.g., she specifically flags that MathsPad 'is well worth the subscription' at her school, and singles out particular features of the X Why graphing tool (bearings diagrams in non-standard orientations) that she found notable.

Her 'Milestone' reflection documents a structural shift in how UK maths teachers share resources: the 2017 GCSE reform coincided with peak activity on teacher-Twitter, and the platform's subsequent decline ('mass exodus of maths teachers from Twitter') has made sourcing material for a monthly gems post measurably harder than it used to be.

The NCETM Key Stage 4 geometry materials entry marks the completion of a multi-year project (the full KS3-KS4 Secondary Mastery Professional Development Materials suite), which Morgan flags as significant for its scope, not just its content.

The piece models a specific professional practice worth noting in its own right: sustained curation of the maths-teaching resource ecosystem by a single practitioner-blogger over more than a decade, with the blog itself functioning as an archive other teachers browse retroactively.
quotes: Welcome to my 200th gems post. This is where I share some of the latest news, ideas and resources for maths teachers.

Their Topic Key Facts Sheets are designed in a two-column question and answer format, so that pupils can self-test by covering up the second column. Very helpful for revision at Key Stage 3 and 4... We love MathsPad at my school - it's well worth the subscription.

I started this blog whilst on maternity leave in April 2014. My first post was about a method for matrix multiplication... I wrote my first gems post in August 2014, when I realised that there were loads of great ideas and resources being shared on Twitter that needed to be shared more widely.

Now I try to write one gems post a month, but it can be difficult to find enough material since the mass exodus of maths teachers from Twitter. Back when the new GCSE was introduced in 2017, social media was packed full of teachers sharing resources and helping each other out.
Today I've published my 518th blog post, which is the 200th post in the Maths Gems series.
I really encourage teachers who meet the criteria to apply for a bursary to help cover the cost - it's so important that teachers attend this conference.
